--- Page 1 ---
Batched Pandora’s Box
Shaddin Dughmi ∗
Yusuf Hakan Kalayci †
Vasilis Livanos ‡
Aditya Prasad §
Abstract
Motivated by numerous parallelizable stochastic search problems, most notable and timely
among them being LLM inference-time scaling, we propose and study batched versions of the
Pandora’s Box problem of Weitzman. In particular, boxes are opened in capacity-constrained
batches, each batch has a setup cost, and all rewards in a batch are revealed together. We
consider two different variants, motivated by different application environments: one where
boxes are reusable (i.e., can provide multiple i.i.d. samples) and another where they are not.
For both variants we rule out most “simple” natural heuristics, and also formally prove NP-
hardness of approximation in the traditional sense. We then relax the problem to allow bi-criteria
approximations, with respect to both rewards and setup costs, where we exhibit constant
approximation algorithms for both the reusable and non-reusable settings. This is obtained
through a linear-programming relaxation of Pandora’s Box problem, followed by randomized or
Pipage rounding.
1
Introduction
In several stochastic search problems, before we find a solution of sufficient quality we need to pay
a search cost. In marketing, a platform tests different advertisements before committing to the
best-performing one; in hyper-parameter tuning, a practitioner trains their model with a menu of
settings before selecting a model; in inference-time reasoning, an inference system issues multiple
LLM queries or decoding strategies before choosing the best response. The classical Pandora’s Box
problem, originally studied by Weitzman [38], captures the sequential version of this tradeoff. Each
option has an inspection cost and an unknown reward, and the decision maker adaptively decides
which option to inspect next and when to stop.
In many of these applications, however, inspections are naturally parallelized. Ad variants in A-B
testing are exposed to users in cohorts, experiments are tested on a pool of machines, and queries to
an LLM are submitted together to reduce latency. This parallelism creates a batched information
structure, as the policy must commit to a set of inspections before seeing any of their outcomes.
A batch may also have a setup cost, capturing the overhead of launching a new experimental
framework, allocating computing resources, or coordinating a marketing campaign. Thus batching
trades off the cost of latency with the savings provided by adaptivity.

--- Page 2 ---
While batched feedback has been studied in bandit problems [31, 18, 23, 36], it has seen
comparatively less study in the Pandora’s Box problem. We initiate this direction by studying a
batched version of the Pandora’s Box problem. In the Batched Pandora’s Box model, we are given n
boxes, each with a distribution of a hidden reward Vi, as well as an opening cost ci. A policy groups
boxes to create the next batch to be opened, and a feasible batch contains at most k boxes for a
given batch capacity k and costs a fixed setup cost T to open in addition to the individual opening
costs. Once a batch is opened, all rewards in the batch are revealed simultaneously. One can then
choose to stop and obtain the maximum reward observed over all opened batches or continue to
open another batch.
We introduce two variants of this model: The non-reusable setting where an opened box is
consumed and cannot be opened again, and the reusable setting where each box can be opened
multiple times and provides a fresh i.i.d. sample each time. The distinction matches the difference
between one-time opportunities, such as allocating a consumer cohort to an ad variant, and repeatable
experiments, such as running additional inference trials of the same LLM. Although this model
is a direct analogue of the classical problem with delayed feedback, the resulting optimization
problem differs significantly from classical Pandora’s Box, requiring us to examine which elements
of Weitzman’s solution to the classical problem carry over to the batched model.
1.1
Our Contributions
We organize our results around three questions raised by batched feedback.
What survives of Weitzman’s index rule under batched feedback?
The answer depends
on reusability. For non-reusable boxes, adaptive batch formation is useful: a policy can choose
later batches after seeing earlier outcomes and thereby outperform every fixed menu of disjoint
batches. This advantage is bounded, however. We prove that every adaptive non-reusable policy
has a fixed-menu counterpart with at least half its value, using a random root-to-leaf path of the
adaptive decision tree in the spirit of stochastic probing [25, 10]. For reusable boxes, we can recover
Weitzman’s index structure. Each feasible batch a has a reservation value σ(a), and an optimal
policy repeatedly opens a maximum-reservation batch until its realized value exceeds that threshold.
Is exact or ordinary approximation tractable?
The answer is negative, in a strong sense.
Specifically, exact optimization is NP-hard for the non-reusable problem for every fixed finite
batch capacity k ≥3. Moreover, with variable batch capacity, and even with k = ∞, both the
non-reusable and reusable models have a sign gap: it is NP-hard to distinguish OPT = 0 from
OPT > 0. The reductions come from Subset Product [19], where the input consists of integers
b1, . . . , bn and a target Q, and the question is whether some subset has product exactly Q. For each
bi, we create a box with a two-point distribution that gives value M with probability 1 −1/bi and
value 0 with probability 1/bi. Hence a batch corresponding to a subset S fails with probability
1/ Q
i∈S bi. By calibrating the setup and item costs, we make it so that a batch has positive surplus
exactly when the product of the constituent boxes’ bi’s is the target Q. Therefore, finding any
positive-value policy certifies a YES instance of Subset Product. This sign gap rules out ordinary
multiplicative approximation under the original costs, since any positive approximation guarantee
would distinguish zero-optimum instances from positive-optimum instances.
Can a discounted-cost relaxation recover useful algorithmic guarantees?
The sign gap
motivates a bi-criteria benchmark: compare against the original-cost optimum, but evaluate the
2


--- Page 3 ---
returned policy with discounted costs. For a policy π, with maximum observed value Mπ and total
cost Cπ, let
valλ(π) = E[Mπ] −λ E[Cπ].
An (α, λ) discounted-cost bi-criteria guarantee means that, for every ε > 0, there is an algorithm
returning an efficient policy bπ = bπ(ε) with
valλ(bπ) ≥α OPT1 −ε,
where OPT1 is the expected value of the optimal adaptive policy with the original (non-discounted)
costs. For finite-support distributions, our algorithms for both variants are based on rounding a
linear programming relaxation of the batched problem. In the non-reusable model, the LP records
opening probabilities, expected batch count, and probabilities that each box is the maximum in a
batch, and upper bounds every nonempty adaptive policy. In a solution of this LP, the batch count
can be fractional, and so we need to round it first to an integral value. Then, we use dependent
rounding to partition the boxes into legal batches. We incur a loss of 2(
√
2 −1) from the batch
count rounding and of 1 −1/e from the correlation gap of the dependent rounding scheme, yielding
in total
valαNR(bπ) ≥αNR OPT1 −ε,
where
αNR = (1 −1/e)2(
√
2 −1).
In the reusable model, we reduce the problem to finding a single batch, corresponding to a multi-set
of boxes, to sample repeatedly until another sample no longer pays for its cost. We design a
feasibility LP RLPτ based on a candidate reservation value of the desired batch that is feasible when
there is a batch certifying a reservation value at least τ. Binary search finds the largest certified
threshold up to a small additive error, and independent slot rounding turns the certificate into an
integral batch. In total, we only incur a rounding loss of αR = 1 −1/e, giving a stronger bound of
valαR(bπ) ≥OPT1 −ε.
1.2
Related Work
Pandora’s Box and costly inspection.
Weitzman’s seminal work [38] initiated study of the
Pandora’s Box setting and showed that independent boxes with inspection costs admit an optimal
reservation-value policy. Subsequent work extends this costly-search view in several directions,
including generalized objectives [30], market-search coordination [28], nonobligatory inspection
[7, 17, 6, 33], combinatorial or online feasibility constraints [34, 8, 5, 9, 13, 12], and correlated
or sample-access variants [15, 14, 22]. Another recent line studies online and learning variants of
Pandora’s Box under online-arrival, contextual, bandit, semi-bandit, and LLM-motivated feedback
models [16, 21, 3, 20, 1, 29, 27, 4]. These works mainly change the distributional knowledge, feedback
available across repeated rounds, contextual structure, or feasible selections. In contrast, our model
is a known-distribution, single-instance Pandora’s Box problem with independent rewards. We keep
the best-observed-value objective and instead change the feedback structure: inspections must be
launched in capacity-limited batches with setup costs.
Stochastic probing and rounding.
Our structural and algorithmic tools also connect to
stochastic probing and submodular rounding. Stochastic probing studies the value of adaptivity
when random elements are probed subject to feasibility constraints, including constant adaptivity
gaps for submodular and XOS objectives and near-optimal results for multi-value probing [25, 10].
Our non-reusable adaptivity-gap proof uses the same random-path perspective, but with Pandora-
specific accounting through reservation values, capped rewards, and fixed-menu Pandora policies.
3


--- Page 4 ---
The LP algorithms use standard correlation-gap and dependent-rounding ideas, including pipage
rounding and correlation-robust stochastic optimization [11, 2].
Delayed feedback.
Delayed feedback has been studied as a natural model in bandits and online
learning. One line of work studies how late observations affect regret in stochastic, Bayesian, or
adversarial bandits, including general delay reductions, delayed conversions, anonymous aggregated
rewards, and unrestricted delays [24, 26, 37, 32, 35, 39]. Another line studies batched or parallel
experimentation, where actions are chosen in groups before feedback from the group is available, for
regret minimization, best-arm identification, or Bayesian optimization [31, 18, 23, 36].
These works share the practical obstruction that decisions may have to be made before earlier
outcomes are observed, but their objective is typically statistical: regret or sample complexity. Our
model is a single-instance search problem. Here delayed feedback enters through capacity-constrained
batches with setup costs, so the delay changes the economics and commitment structure of costly
inspection rather than only the rate at which a learner receives information.
2
Preliminaries
In the classical Pandora’s Box problem, there are n boxes numbered [n] = {1, . . . , n}. Box i has
an independent non-negative reward Vi with finite mean and a deterministic opening cost ci ≥0.
Opening box i costs ci and immediately reveals Vi. Weitzman’s rule assigns each box a reservation
value
τi = sup
n
τ ∈R : E
(Vi −τ)+ ≥ci
o
,
opens boxes in decreasing order of τi, and stops when the best observed reward is at least as large
as the largest remaining reservation value [38].
Model.
We study a batched version of this problem. We group the boxes into batches where each
batch contains at most k boxes and, to open a nonempty batch, we have to pay a setup cost T ≥0
in addition to the individual opening costs. When a batch is opened, all rewards in it are revealed
together. We consider two variants: a non-reusable model, as in the classical problem, where opened
boxes are consumed and thus batches partition the boxes, and a reusable model, where each box
can provide multiple i.i.d. samples and thus batches correspond to multisets of boxes.
Definition 2.1 (Non-Reusable Batched Pandora’s Box, BP(T, k)). A feasible batch is a nonempty
subset B of currently unopened boxes with |B| ≤k. Opening B costs
K(B) = T +
X
i∈B
ci,
reveals (Vi)i∈B, and consumes all boxes in B. If k = ∞, the cardinality constraint is omitted.
Since the batches partition the n boxes in the non-reusable model, BP(T, k) is identical to
BP(T, n) whenever k ≥n.
Definition 2.2 (Reusable Batched Pandora’s Box, RBP(T, k)). Each box type i ∈[n] has a strictly
positive sampling cost ci > 0.1 A feasible reusable batch is a vector a ∈Zn
≥0 of multiplicities with
1 ≤∥a∥1 ≤k. Opening a costs
K(a) = T +
X
i
aici
1This assumption is relevant only when k = ∞; it rules out degenerate instances in which arbitrarily many copies
of a zero-cost type can be included without increasing the batch cost.
4


--- Page 5 ---
and draws ai i.i.d. samples of type i. The reward observed in batch a is
Xa = max
i∈[n] max
1≤r≤ai Vi,r,
where Vi,r denotes the r-th sample of type i. Since boxes (and thus batches) are reusable, they
remain available to be used in later rounds. If k = ∞, the cardinality constraint is omitted.
For a policy π in any of these models, let Mπ be the maximum reward observed by the policy,
with Mπ = 0 if no box is opened, and let Cπ be the total cost paid, including setup and individual
opening costs. As in the classical problem, we evaluate the performance of a policy π by its expected
maximum reward minus its expected total cost. We define the discounted-cost value
valλ(π) = E[Mπ] −λ E[Cπ],
where λ ∈[0, 1]. Thus, λ = 1 corresponds to the original-cost objective, while λ < 1 corresponds
to evaluating the policy after discounting the costs. We refer to val1(π) as the utility of policy
π. Similarly, the utility of a batch — also called its one-shot surplus — is its expected maximum
reward minus its opening cost. We write OPT1 for the optimal original-cost value, taking the empty
policy when the optimum is zero. The source of the main departure of our batched model from the
classical Pandora’s Box is the setup cost.
Observation 2.3. When T = 0, any chosen batch can be simulated by opening its boxes sequentially,
ignoring intermediate observations until the batch is complete; the same applies to the fresh samples
in a reusable batch. Since singleton batches (batches of size 1) are feasible, for every k ≥1, BP(0, k)
has the classical singleton value (i.e. BP(0, k) = BP(0, 1)), and if ci > 0 for every i, then RBP(0, k)
has the reusable singleton value (i.e. RBP(0, k) = RBP(0, 1)).
Computational considerations.
We represent each distribution by a finite list of value-
probability pairs (viℓ, piℓ), where viℓ≥0, piℓ> 0, and P
ℓpiℓ= 1. We use Li for the (non-zero)
support of the distribution of box i, i.e. ℓ∈Li =⇒viℓ> 0. The hardness reductions use two-point
distributions, while all approximation statements are stated for this finite-support input model.
Submodular functions.
For a set function f : 2[n] →R≥0, we say that f is normalized if
f(∅) = 0, monotone if f(A) ≤f(B) for all A ⊆B, and submodular if, for all A ⊆B ⊆[n] and
i /∈B,
f(A ∪{i}) −f(A) ≥f(B ∪{i}) −f(B).
The function F(x) = E[f(Sx)] is called the multilinear extension of f, where Sx includes each
element i independently with probability xi.
3
Structural Observations
We begin by examining how the index-based structure of Weitzman’s policy changes under batching.
A natural first attempt greedily merges boxes in order of decreasing reservation values. We show
that this type of sort-and-merge consecutive boxes policy fails badly: in our construction, the only
positive utility batch combines a non-consecutive group of boxes. Here, the optimal policy’s batches
can be made arbitrarily far apart. This rules out both greedy and dynamic programming approaches
for partitioning the boxes into consecutive batches in the reservation-value order.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Next, we examine the strength of adaptivity. In the non-reusable model, we present an example
that establishes a gap between the value attained by adaptive policies and fixed-menu policies that
commit to a partition of boxes into batches and run Weitzman’s policy on the fixed batches. Then,
we show that this adaptivity gap between the two types of policies can be at most a factor of 2.
Finally, we show that in the reusable setting, there is no gap between the optimal adaptive and
non-adaptive policy. As a nice byproduct, we recover an index principle in the style of Weitzman:
specifically, the optimal policy repeats the batch with the highest reservation value until the batch
value exceeds the reservation threshold.
3.1
Failure of Simple Batching Rules
A natural first attempt is to import Weitzman’s ordering rule into the batched problem. Compute
each box’s reservation value as if it were opened alone, sort boxes in decreasing order of these
values, and then form batches from consecutive blocks of this order. This preserves the intuition
that high-index boxes should be inspected early and, in the batched setting, possibly inspected
together. The next example shows that this rule misses a batched effect: setup costs can make two
separated boxes valuable together even though every consecutive batch in the reservation-value
order is unprofitable.
Take T = 10 and k = 2.
Let A have item cost cA = 1, with Pr[VA = 100] = 0.1 and
Pr[VA = 0] = 0.9. Let B be deterministic with value 9, with item cost cB = 1. Individually, neither
box pays for the setup cost. However, together they have expected maximum
E[max{VA, VB}] = 0.1 · 100 + 0.9 · 9 = 18.1,
so the batch {A, B} has positive utility. We will design the instance so that the target boxes A and
B will be arbitrarily far apart under Weitzman’s reservation-value ordering.
Now consider a deterministic decoy box D. Let D have value 100 and item cost cD = 91. Its
reservation value is worse than A’s but better than B’s, so the sorted order is A ≻D ≻B. At the
same time, D never contributes a useful net value: it duplicates the high outcome of A, but its item
cost is almost as large as its value. One can verify that every feasible consecutive batch has negative
utility, while {A, B} has positive utility. Therefore, no consecutive batching algorithm, whether
greedy or based on dynamic programming over intervals, can obtain positive utility on this example.
The exact calculations are given in Section A.1, which also proves a stronger bi-criteria lower bound:
for every batch capacity k ≥2 and every α > 1/2, no algorithm restricted to consecutive batches in
the reservation-value order can guarantee an (α, α)-bi-criteria approximation.
3.2
Non-Reusable Model: Adaptivity Gap
A fixed-menu policy first commits to a disjoint family F of feasible batches. It then treats each
batch B ∈F as one box in a finite classical Pandora instance, with reward XB = maxi∈B Vi and cost
K(B), and applies Weitzman’s rule. Let OPTfix(T, k) denote the best value of any such fixed-menu
policy. This benchmark preserves the Pandora stopping rule while removing the branching structure
of adaptive batch choice.
The natural question is whether the best fixed menu can match the value of the best adaptive
policy. For k = 1 the answer is yes, by the classical Pandora rule. For larger batches, fixed menus
lose the ability to branch on an early observation before deciding which later batch to open. The
following example shows that this restriction can reduce value.
Example 3.1 (Adaptive branching can help). Consider three boxes with setup cost T = 1/5 and
batch capacity k = 2. Box 1 is deterministic with value 1/2. Box 2 is 0 with probability 2/5, 1/2
6


--- Page 7 ---
with probability 2/5, and 9 with probability 1/5. Box 3 is 10 with probability 1/5, and 0 otherwise.
The item costs are c1 = c2 = 1
5 and c3 = 1.
The adaptive policy first opens box 2. If box 2 realizes as 9, the policy stops. If box 2 realizes
as 1/2, it opens box 3 alone. If box 2 realizes as 0, it opens the batch {1, 3}. The point is that box
1 is useful only if box 3 realizes as 0, i.e. when we don’t already have a guarantee from box 2.
A fixed menu cannot make this branch-dependent choice. It must decide in advance whether box
1 is grouped with box 3, separated from box 3, or grouped with box 2. For this instance, the adaptive
policy has value 57/25 = 2.28, whereas the best fixed-menu policy has value 279/125 = 2.232. Thus
adaptive branching strictly improves over every fixed menu. Appendix A.2 gives a tuned version of
the same signal/fallback/risky-box template, with all parameters rounded to two decimal places; in
that instance, the adaptive policy attains about 1.193 times the value of the best fixed-menu policy.
Nevertheless, the value of adaptive batch formation is bounded: every adaptive policy is within
a constant factor of the best fixed-menu policy.
Theorem 3.2 (Non-Reusable Adaptivity Gap). For every T and k,
OPTBP(T,k)
1
≤2 · OPTfix(T, k).
The proof is existential and is given in Section A. It utilizes a random-path rounding argument
in the style of stochastic probing [25, 10]: one samples a root-to-leaf path of the adaptive decision
tree on an independent “ghost” instance and then plays that fixed path on the real instance. For
this style of argument, we must ensure that along any realization of box values, the batches consist
of disjoint sets of boxes. Then, we use Weitzman’s capped-value analysis to turn this path into a
fixed-menu policy losing at most a factor two.
3.3
Reusable boxes: one repeated batch
We turn our attention to the reusable setting. Since opening a reusable batch does not consume
future access to it, each reusable batch can be viewed as a box with infinitely many independent
copies. The dynamic problem therefore reduces to identifying the batch with the largest reservation
value. For a reusable batch a, recall that Xa is the best reward among the fresh copies drawn by
opening a, and K(a) is its setup-plus-sampling cost. If 0 < K(a) ≤E[Xa], define its reservation
value σ(a) by K(a) = E
(Xa −σ(a))+. Batches with K(a) > E[Xa] are overpriced. Let
σ⋆= max

{0} ∪{σ(a) : a is feasible and not overpriced}

.
Theorem 3.3 (Reusable Reservation Index). Assume values lie in [0, Vmax] and every non-empty
feasible batch has positive opening cost. For k = ∞, also assume every ci > 0. If σ⋆= 0, opening
nothing is optimal. If σ⋆> 0, then for any feasible batch a⋆with σ(a⋆) = σ∗, the policy that
repeatedly opens a⋆until it observes a reward exceeding σ⋆is optimal.
The theorem is the reusable analogue of Weitzman’s index rule. A copy of the best reservation
batch remains available after every failed attempt, so the index policy continues to choose it. The
boundedness and positive-cost assumptions ensure that the relevant batches that are not overpriced
are finite in number; the formal details are in Section A.
The repeated-batch value equals the reservation value. If batch a has reservation value σ(a) and
p = Pr[Xa > σ(a)], then repeatedly opening it until the first success gives
E[Xa | Xa > σ(a)] −K(a)
p
= E[Xa1{Xa > σ(a)}]
p
−K(a)
p
= σ(a) + E[(Xa −σ(a))+] −K(a)
p
= σ(a).

The last equality uses E[(Xa −σ(a))+] = K(a), by the definition of σ(a).
4
Hardness Results
In this section, we show that the various settings of Batched Pandora’s Box are NP-hard. Broadly,
our reductions construct instances of Batched Pandora’s Box in which even building a batch with
positive utility encodes NP-hard search problems.
Product gadget.
Our reductions use a common product gadget. Each box has the same positive
prize M, and the box corresponding to label bi fails with probability 1/bi. A batch whose labels
multiply to weight w = Q
i∈B bi then fails with probability 1/w. We set the item costs and the
batching cost carefully as a function of the weights of the boxes, ensuring a batch offers positive
opening utility if and only if its labels multiply to a prescribed target value Q. Consequently, finding
a batch with positive opening utility encodes an NP-hard search problem, yielding hardness for
Batched Pandora’s Box. For clarity, we initially present the proof using exact logarithms, and
then show that rational approximations to the logarithms (of polynomial length) still preserve this
property. The formal proofs are presented in Section 6.
Non-reusable boxes.
We first investigate the non-reusable problem. Exact optimization is
already intractable for every fixed finite batch capacity at least three.
Theorem 4.1 (Fixed Finite-Batch-Capacity Exact Hardness). For every fixed k ≥3, exact
optimization of BP(T, k) is NP-hard, even when T > 0 and all boxes have support {0, M} for a
shared M. Equivalently, deciding whether OPT1 ≥Θ for a rational threshold Θ is NP-hard.
We reduce from the strongly NP-hard Numerical 3-Dimensional Matching problem. The instance
consists of three classes of items X, Y, Z and a size function s(e), e ∈X ∪Y ∪Z, and the goal is to
partition the items into triples (x, y, z) satisfying s(x) + s(y) + s(z) = B.
For batch size k = 3, we encode each item e as a box whose label contains the factor 2s(e). To
encode the class constraint, we assign a distinct identifying prime to each of X, Y, Z, and include
the corresponding prime in the label of every item from that class. We then set the target product
to be the product of the three class primes times 2B. By unique factorization, a batch has the target
product if and only if it contains one item from each class whose sizes sum to B. For k > 3, we add
dummy zero-size classes to fill the remaining positions in each batch.
The product gadget makes precisely the target tuples profitable. Since all target tuples have the
same success probability and the same cost, the optimal value is a strictly increasing function of the
maximum number of disjoint target tuples, and exact optimization distinguishes whether a perfect
numerical matching exists.
The next question is whether one can at least obtain an ordinary constant-factor approxima-
tion. When batch capacity is part of the input, the product gadget gives a stronger obstruction:
distinguishing zero value from positive value is already NP-hard.
Theorem 4.2 (Non-Reusable Sign-Gap Decision Hardness). For BP(T, k) with k part of the input,
and for BP(T, ∞), the promise problem of distinguishing
OPT1 = 0
from
OPT1 > 0
is NP-hard, even on common-prize two-point instances with T > 0.
8


--- Page 9 ---
Here the reduction is from Subset Product: given labels a1, . . . , an and target Q, decide
whether some subset has product Q. The batch capacity is set to the number of source items. If
a target subset exists, opening the corresponding batch once gives positive value; otherwise every
nonempty batch has negative one-shot surplus. Because all boxes have a common prize, adaptive
stopping cannot turn these negative-surplus attempts into positive value: before the first success the
policy observes only zeros, and the expected reward from any sequence of attempts is dominated by
its expected cost.
Reusable boxes.
For reusable boxes, the same product idea applies, but we must prevent a
target batch from using multiple copies of the same source item. Broadly, for each source item i,
we introduce a private prime pi and create two boxes whose labels correspond to pi and piai. We
set the target product to Q Q
i pi. Since pi appears in no other label and has exponent one in the
target, any multi-set whose labels multiply to the target must contain exactly one of pi and piai for
each i. Choosing pi corresponds to excluding ai from the subset, while choosing piai corresponds to
including it. After canceling the private primes, the remaining condition enforces that the product
of the selected ai’s equals Q. Finally, the product gadget then gives the reusable sign gap.
Theorem 4.3 (Reusable Sign-Gap Decision Hardness). For RBP(T, k) with finite k as part of the
input, and for RBP(T, ∞), the promise problem of distinguishing
OPT1 = 0
from
OPT1 > 0
is NP-hard, even on common-prize two-point instances with T > 0.
For unbounded batch capacity, item costs make all sufficiently large multisets automatically
overpriced, so the reduction only has to protect a finite range of multiplicities by the product
separation.
5
Bi-criteria Approximation Results
The hardness results of the previous section preclude standard positive-factor approximation
guarantees under the original costs. We therefore turn to discounted-cost bicriteria guarantees.
Recall that valλ(π) = E[Mπ] −λ E[Cπ], and that an algorithm has an (α, λ) guarantee if, for every
requested ε > 0, it returns a feasible policy bπ = bπ(ε) with valλ(bπ) ≥α OPT1 −ε. Thus, the
algorithm is compared with the original-cost optimum, while its returned policy is evaluated after
discounting costs.
5.1
Non-Reusable Boxes
Consider first the non-reusable model. Although an adaptive policy may have a possibly exponential
decision tree, before any values are realized, it induces only ex-ante statistics: the probability xi that
each box is ever opened and the expected number z of batches it opens. These statistics determine
the expected cost. The relaxation therefore only needs to upper-bound the final reward that can be
attributed to the opened boxes. For each box i, we omit the zero atom and, for ℓ∈Li, write
Pr[Vi = viℓ] = piℓ,
where
viℓ> 0.
When box i is the final selected value and realizes as the point viℓin its support, we assign the
probability mass of this event to a variable yiℓ. This “winner” event can occur only if box i is
9


--- Page 10 ---
Algorithm 1 Non-reusable LP rounding
Input: Opening marginals x, fractional batch count z ≥1, and capacity k
Set θ = z −⌊z⌋
Draw ¯z = ⌊z⌋with probability 1 −θ, and ¯z = ⌈z⌉with probability θ
Set qi = min{1, (¯z/z)xi} for every box i
Apply pipage rounding over the rank-(k¯z) uniform matroid to obtain a set S with |S| ≤k¯z
Partition S arbitrarily into at most ¯z groups of size at most k each, open all nonempty groups,
and stop

give the following relaxation:

The constraint P
i xi ≤kz is the ex-ante version of batch capacity: if a policy opens z batches in
expectation, it cannot open more than kz boxes in expectation.
At first glance, one could think that we could write n different versions of this LP, one per
candidate value of z, since any policy always opens an integer number of batches, and take the
maximum of these n LPs. This, in principle, would save us the extra loss we incur from rounding z.
Unfortunately, such an approach does not constitute a valid upper bound to the optimal adaptive
policy, since the latter could open a different number of batches depending on the history of observed
values and thus, in expectation, a fractional number of batches overall. For this reason, allowing z
to be fractional is crucial so that the LP can capture the value of the optimal adaptive algorithm.
Also, the LP is a relaxation for the optimal adaptive algorithm, because the atom masses are allowed
to be arranged fractionally into a final winning value. After fixing the opening marginals x, this
upper bound on the expected reward has the equivalent threshold form
B(x) =
Z ∞
0
min
(
1,
X
i
xi Pr[Vi > t]
)
dt.
Sampling which boxes to open independently with probabilities given by the xi’s guarantees a
(1−1/e)-fraction of this envelope at every threshold. Afterwards, pipage rounding algorithm converts
the opening marginals x into an actual set of opened boxes, while respecting the batch budget
certified by z, without decreasing the expected monotone submodular reward.
We also round z to one of its two neighboring integers and scale the opening marginals accordingly.
Once the number of batches is integral, a selected set of at most k¯z boxes can be partitioned arbitrarily
into ¯z legal batches. Consequently, the rounding incurs only the batch-count factor 2(
√
2 −1) from
rounding the batch count and no additional contention loss inside individual batches.

instance and every ε > 0, there is a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that returns a policy

The algorithm solves (LP), returns the empty policy if its optimum is non-positive, and otherwise
applies Algorithm 1 to an optimal solution.
The proof follows this outline. The details are in Section 7.1.
5.2
Reusable Boxes
The reusable case starts from a different structural fact. By Theorem 3.3, an optimal original-cost
policy repeats one maximum-reservation batch. Thus, it suffices to find one certifying multiset of at
most k fresh i.i.d. samples. The case T = 0 is handled exactly by Observation 2.3, so assume T > 0
below and let Vmax be the largest support value.
For a threshold τ, write fτ(a) = E[(Xa −τ)+]. If one batch pays for its discounted cost using
the expected excess above τ, then repeatedly opening it guarantees discounted value at least τ.
Lemma 5.2 (Threshold Certificate). Fix λ ∈(0, 1]. If a nonempty reusable batch a satisfies
fτ(a) ≥λK(a),
then repeatedly opening a until the first realization Xa > τ has λ-discounted value at least τ.
This observation reduces the reusable algorithm to a threshold search. For a candidate τ, the
task is to determine whether some batch can certify it, i.e. whether there is a batch with reservation
value at least τ. The fractional relaxation is similar to the non-reusable LP, except that it is turned
into a feasibility LP and xi is now a fractional number of copies of type i in a single reusable batch:
find
x, y
s.t.
X
i
xi ≤k,
0 ≤yiℓ≤piℓxi
∀i, ℓ∈Li,
0 ≤xi
∀i,
X
i
X
ℓ∈Li
yiℓ≤1
X
i
X
ℓ∈Li
(viℓ−τ)+yiℓ≥T +
X
i
cixi
(RLPτ)
We say that τ is LP-certified if RLPτ is feasible. The y-variables form a fractional one-winner
certificate: the constraints yiℓ≤piℓxi encode the marginal availability of atom viℓ, while P
i,ℓyiℓ≤1
encodes that one batch contributes only one maximum value. Thus feasibility of RLPτ certifies that
the fractional excess above τ can pay for the batch cost. Lowering τ only increases the coefficients
(viℓ−τ)+ and makes the certificate constraint easier to satisfy. Therefore, certification is monotone
and binary search can find the largest certified threshold up to an additive error.
When a threshold is certified fractionally, we round by filling the k batch slots independently
according to the copy counts xi. At level t ≥τ, one slot exceeds t with probability P
i xi Pr[Vi > t]/k,
so the rounded batch achieves an αR = 1 −1/e fraction of the fractional excess envelope. The
method of conditional expectations derandomizes the slot choices without losing the certificate.

--- Page 12 ---
Algorithm 2 Reusable threshold search
Input: A finite-support reusable RBP(T, k) instance and accuracy ε > 0
Set ℓ= 0, u = Vmax, bτ = 0, and ba = 0
for ⌈log2(Vmax/ε)⌉iterations do
Set τ = (ℓ+ u)/2 and solve RLPτ
if τ is LP-certified then
Round feasible LP solution into a certifying batch aτ using the method of conditional
expectation
Set ℓ= τ, bτ = τ, and ba = aτ
else
Set u = τ
end if
end for
if ba = 0 then
return the empty policy
end if
Repeatedly open ba until its value exceeds bτ
Theorem 5.3 (Finite-Support Reusable Guarantee). For every finite-support reusable instance
with finite batch capacity k and every ε > 0, Algorithm 2 runs in polynomial time and returns a
policy bπ = bπ(ε) satisfying
valαR(bπ) ≥OPT1 −ε,
αR = 1 −1
e.
Equivalently, the algorithm provides a (1, αR) discounted-cost bicriteria guarantee.
The comparison with the optimum follows from the reusable reservation-index theorem. If a⋆
is an optimal original-cost batch with reservation value OPT1, then it certifies every threshold
τ ≤OPT1 in the feasibility LP. Binary search therefore reaches a threshold within ε of the optimum,
and the rounded certifying batch is converted into a repeated policy by Lemma 5.2. The formal
proof appears in Section 7.2.

We will repeatedly use two numerical primitives. First, define

Second, we will use rational approximations to logarithms so that all constructed costs are

Lemma 6.2 (Rational Log Approximation). Let m1, . . . , mr be positive integers and let η > 0 be
rational. In time polynomial in the input bit length and log(1/η), one can compute rational numbers
ℓ1, . . . , ℓr such that
|ℓi −ln mi| ≤η
for all i.
Proof. The approximation claim is the standard bit-complexity computation of elementary functions:
after range reduction, logarithms can be approximated to b bits by classical polynomial-time series
or binary-splitting algorithms.
6.1
Proof of Theorem 4.1: Fixed finite-capacity non-reusable boxes
Proof of Theorem 4.1. We first describe the reduction using exact logarithmic costs and ignore
representation-size issues; the final paragraph replaces the logarithms by rational approximations
and checks that the constructed instance has polynomial encoding length. We reduce from strongly
NP-complete Numerical 3-Dimensional Matching [19]. An instance consists of three classes X, Y, Z,
each of size m, positive integer sizes s(e), and a target B. The question is whether the elements can
be partitioned into m triples (x, y, z) satisfying
s(x) + s(y) + s(z) = B.
Since Numerical 3DM is strongly NP-complete, we may restrict to instances in which B and all sizes
s(e) are bounded by a polynomial in m. We also assume m ≥2, since the case m = 1 is decidable
directly.

containing m dummy elements of size zero. Choose k distinct odd primes p1, . . . , pk, one per class,

Let ν be the maximum number of pairwise-disjoint target batches. By Lemma A.2, an optimal
policy opens only target batches. Until the first success, every observed value is zero, so the all-failure
path of any deterministic policy is a sequence of disjoint target batches and has length at most ν.
Conversely, any packing of r target batches can be opened in any order until the first success. Its
expected utility is
M · (1 −qr) −K · (1 + q + · · · + qr−1) =
␀M · (1 −q) −K
 · (1 + q + · · · + qr−1)
= ∆· (1 + q + · · · + qr−1).
This expression is strictly increasing in r. Randomization and stopping before exhausting a packing
cannot improve it, since every additional available target batch has the same positive conditional
surplus. Hence
OPT1 = ∆· (1 + q + · · · + qν−1),
with the geometric sum interpreted as zero when ν = 0.

so the threshold Θ is polynomially representable. Thus the rational instance and threshold are
produced in polynomial time.

6.2
Proof of Theorem 4.2: Sign-gap hardness for non-reusable boxes
Before proving the non-reusable sign-gap theorem, we isolate the batch-level hardness used in the
reduction. For a feasible batch B, let XB be the best value observed inside the batch and let K(B)
be its opening cost. Its one-shot surplus is
∆(B) = E[XB] −K(B).
If ∆(B) < 0, equivalently K(B) > E[XB], the batch is overpriced.
The construction makes the probability of no success equal to the reciprocal of a product. Costs
are logarithmic in the same labels. Thus the reward term contributes a reciprocal-product term,
the cost term contributes a logarithmic term, and after calibration the surplus contains D(w/Q),
which is uniquely minimized at the target product w = Q.
Definition 6.3 (Restricted Subset Product). The input consists of integers a1, . . . , an ≥2 and
an integer target Q ≥8. The question is whether there is a subset S ⊆[n] such that
Y
i∈S
ai = Q.
The usual Subset Product problem has no restrictions on ai or Q. The restricted version
above remains NP-hard.
Lemma 6.4 (Restricted Subset Product Remains NP-Hard). Restricted Subset Product is
NP-hard.
Proof. Reduce from the standard Subset Product problem. Given an instance (a1, . . . , an, Q),
delete all labels equal to 1, since they do not affect feasibility, and write
A =
Y
i
ai
for the product of the remaining labels, with A = 1 if none remain. Add one new label
P = 8 · A
and set the new target to
Q′ = P · Q.
All labels in the new instance are at least 2, and Q′ ≥8.
If the original instance has a subset of product Q, then adding the new label P gives a subset of
product Q′. Conversely, any subset of the new instance with product Q′ must contain P: without
it, the product is at most A < Q′. After removing P, the remaining selected labels have product Q.
Thus the two instances are equivalent, and the transformation has polynomial bit length because
log A is at most the total input length.

instance contains a nonempty positive-surplus feasible batch is NP-hard, even when the batch capacity
is part of the input and also when k = ∞, and even with T > 0.

issues; the final paragraph replaces the logarithms by rational approximations and checks that the

Proof of Theorem 4.2. Use the instances constructed in Lemma 6.5 with H = 1. In a YES instance,
there is a batch with positive one-shot surplus, so opening it once gives OPT1 > 0. In a NO instance,
every nonempty feasible batch is overpriced. By Lemma A.2, there is an optimal non-reusable policy
that never opens an overpriced batch. Hence the empty policy is optimal and OPT1 = 0. Thus a
polynomial-time solver for the promise problem would decide the NP-hard batch-existence problem
from Lemma 6.5.

Proof of Theorem 4.3: Sign-gap hardness for reusable boxes
Lemma 6.6. For every rational H > 0, deciding whether a common-prize high-or-zero reusable
instance contains a nonempty positive-surplus feasible batch is NP-hard when finite k is part of the
input, and also for k = ∞, even with T > 0.
Proof. We first describe the reduction using exact logarithmic costs and ignore representation-size
issues; the final paragraph replaces the logarithms by rational approximations and checks that the
constructed instance has polynomial encoding length. We reduce from restricted Subset Product.
Let the source instance be (a1, . . . , an, Q). The only additional difficulty in the reusable model is
that a batch may contain repeated copies. We first encode each original item as a forced binary
choice, so that any product hitting the target uses each source item at most once.

has a positive-surplus feasible batch if and only if the source Subset Product instance is YES.
The private primes can be found in polynomial time: if Lin is the total source bit length, then
Q · Q
j aj has at most Lin distinct prime divisors, so among the first n + Lin primes at least n
are available. Thus the primes, labels, and target Q′ have polynomial binary encoding length. In
the unbounded-batch-capacity case, L0 = 4Q′ + 1 may be numerically large, but its bit length is
polynomial. The required precision has polynomial encoding length. The exact setup cost is positive
for Q′ ≥8, and replacing ln Q′ by its rational approximation changes it by at most Λδ ≤H/100, so
the setup cost remains positive. Hence the rational instance is produced in polynomial time.
Proof of Theorem 4.3. Use the instances constructed in Lemma 6.6 with H = 1. In a YES instance,
there is a reusable batch with positive one-shot surplus. For a common-prize reusable batch with
success probability s, cost K, and prize M, positive surplus means K < sM, so its reservation value
is M −K/s > 0. By Theorem 3.3, this gives OPT1 > 0. In a NO instance, every nonempty reusable
batch is overpriced. Then σ⋆= 0, and Theorem 3.3 says opening nothing is optimal, so OPT1 = 0.
Thus a polynomial-time solver for the promise problem would decide the NP-hard batch-existence
problem from Lemma 6.6.

Proofs of Bicriteria Approximation Results
7.1
Proof of Theorem 5.1: Non-reusable boxes
The proof follows the outline from Section 5.1. We first identify the finite-support reward envelope,
then verify that every adaptive policy induces a feasible LP point, and finally analyze the rounding
of the opening marginals and the fractional batch count.
For fixed opening marginals x ∈[0, 1]n, define the atomized one-winner envelope
B(x) = max




With this envelope in place, the next step is to check that the LP is indeed a relaxation of
adaptive policies. This is where the nonanticipatory nature of a policy is used: the decision to open
box i is made before the realization of Vi is observed.
When upper-bounding a positive-utility policy, it is without loss of generality to assume that
the policy opens its first batch with probability one. Indeed, if a policy stops immediately with
probability 1 −q and otherwise follows a nonempty policy π′, then
val1(π) = q val1(π′).
Thus, whenever val1(π) > 0, conditioning on the nonempty branch weakly increases utility.
20


--- Page 21 ---

batch with probability one induces a feasible LP solution with objective value E[Mπ] −E[Cπ].

After the number of batches is integral, the remaining requirement is the ex-post capacity bound.
Since capacity is uniform and batches can be formed after the set is chosen, pipage rounding supplies
the final conversion from fractional marginals to a feasible set.
Lemma 7.5 (Uniform-Capacity Pipage Rounding). Let f : 2[n] →R≥0 be normalized, monotone,
and submodular, with multilinear extension F. If q ∈[0, 1]n and P

rounding returns S with |S| ≤K, Pr[i ∈S] = qi, and
E[f(S)] ≥F(q).
This is the standard pipage-rounding guarantee for monotone submodular functions under a
uniform matroid constraint [11].

The LP has polynomially many variables and constraints in the finite-support input representation.

time.
7.2
Proof of Theorem 5.3: Reusable boxes
The reusable proof follows the same order as the overview in Section 5.2. First, a threshold certificate
is converted into an actual repeated policy. Then we show that the feasibility LP contains every
integral batch certificate, and finally that a fractional certificate can be rounded to an integral batch
while losing only the discounted-cost factor.
Proof of Lemma 5.2. Let p = Pr[Xa > τ]. The certificate implies p > 0. Repeating a until the first
threshold crossing uses a geometric number of openings, so its λ-discounted value is
E[Xa | Xa > τ] −λK(a)
p
= τ + fτ(a) −λK(a)
p
≥τ.
The threshold certificate is useful only if the relaxation certifies every integral batch that could
serve as the optimal repeated batch. The next lemma checks this by assigning the selected excess
above threshold to the atom that realizes it.

Lemma 7.6 (RLPτ Relaxes Integral Batches). Let a be a feasible reusable batch with reservation
value σ(a). Then, for every τ ≤σ(a), there exist variables yiℓsuch that xi = ai and (x, y) is feasible
for RLPτ.
Proof. Set xi = ai. After one opening of a, break ties deterministically among copies whose value is
the batch maximum and exceeds τ. If the maximum is at most τ, select no atom. Otherwise, let
the selected winning copy have type i and atom viℓ, and define yiℓas the probability of this event.
Then P

Therefore the certificate constraint of RLPτ is satisfied, and (x, y), with xi = ai, is feasible for
RLPτ.
Conversely, a certified fractional solution must be implemented as a true batch. We fill the k

It remains to combine threshold monotonicity, slot rounding, and the structural characterization
of optimal reusable policies by a single reservation-index batch.
Theorem 5.3 (Finite-Support Reusable Guarantee). For every finite-support reusable instance
with finite batch capacity k and every ε > 0, Algorithm 2 runs in polynomial time and returns a
policy bπ = bπ(ε) satisfying
valαR(bπ) ≥OPT1 −ε,
αR = 1 −1
e.
Equivalently, the algorithm provides a (1, αR) discounted-cost bicriteria guarantee.
Proof. The case T = 0 is handled exactly by Observation 2.3, so assume T > 0. Certification is
monotone: if τ is LP-certified, then every τ ′ ≤τ is also LP-certified, because lowering the threshold
increases the coefficients (viℓ−τ)+ and makes the certificate constraint easier to satisfy.

Since the input distributions have finite support, the conditional expectation of the displayed
certificate can be computed exactly after any partial assignment of slots. The method of conditional
expectations returns a realization a satisfying
fτ(a) ≥αRK(a).
Because T > 0, the all-dummy realization has negative certificate value, so the returned batch is
nonempty. By Lemma 5.2, the repeated policy for this batch has αR-discounted value at least τ.
If OPT1 = 0, the algorithm either returns the empty policy or a certified repeated batch, both
of which have nonnegative αR-discounted value. Suppose OPT1 > 0. By Theorem 3.3, there is an
optimal reusable batch a⋆with reservation value σ⋆= OPT1. For every τ ≤σ⋆,
fτ(a⋆) ≥fσ⋆(a⋆) = K(a⋆).
Lemma 7.6 therefore implies that every τ ≤OPT1 is LP-certified. Monotonicity of certification lets
binary search return a certified threshold bτ ≥OPT1 −ε. The policy returned for bτ satisfies
valαR(bπ) ≥bτ ≥OPT1 −ε.

Additional Structural Details
A.1
A lower bound for consecutive batching
We sort boxes by their individual reservation values computed with respect to item costs only: σi is
defined by
E[(Vi −σi)+] = ci.
Fix an ordering of the boxes. A consecutive-batch policy is a policy that only opens intervals in the
current remaining order.
We first give the full calculation for the example from the main text. The setup cost is T = 10,
the batch capacity is k = 2, and the boxes are ordered as A, D, B. Box A has item cost cA = 1,
with Pr[VA = 100] = 0.1 and Pr[VA = 0] = 0.9. Box B is deterministic with value 9 and item cost
cB = 1. Box D is deterministic with value 100 and item cost cD = 91.
The reservation values are
σA = 100 −1
0.1 = 90,
σD = 100 −91 = 9,
σB = 9 −1 = 8.
Thus the reservation-value order is A ≻D ≻B. The utilities of the consecutive feasible batches are
S
{A}
{D}
{B}
{A, D}
{D, B}
u(S)
−1
−1
−2
−2
−2.
Indeed, u({A}) = 10 −10 −1 = −1, u({D}) = 100 −10 −91 = −1, u({B}) = 9 −10 −1 = −2, and
both pairs containing D have maximum value 100 and total cost 102. On the other hand,
u({A, B}) = E[max{VA, VB}] −10 −1 −1 =
␀0.1 · 100 + 0.9 · 9
 −10 −1 −1 = 6.1 > 0.
So the non-consecutive batch {A, B} is profitable, while every consecutive batch is unprofitable.
Moreover, every consecutive-batch policy has value at most zero. If such a policy ever opens D,
then its final reward is at most 100, while opening D alone already costs T + cD = 101. Thus any
policy opening D has negative value. If the policy never opens D, then it can only open A and B as
singleton batches. The expected marginal reward from opening A is at most 10 < T + cA = 11, and
the expected marginal reward from opening B is at most 9 < T + cB = 11. Hence opening either
singleton cannot increase expected value, and the empty policy is optimal among consecutive-batch
policies.
We now prove the bicriteria lower bound.
Theorem A.1. Fix k ≥2 and α ∈(1/2, 1]. There is a finite-support non-reusable instance with
setup cost T = 1 and batch capacity k such that the reservation-value order is
A ≻D1 ⪰· · · ⪰Dk ≻B,
where D1, . . . , Dk are identical decoy boxes, and every consecutive-batch policy π satisfies
valα(π) ≤0,
while OPT1 > 0. Consequently, no algorithm restricted to consecutive batches in this order can
guarantee an (α, α)-bicriteria approximation for any α > 1/2.
29


--- Page 30 ---
Proof. The construction has two useful boxes and a block of decoy boxes. The useful boxes A and
B are profitable only when opened together: A is a rare large prize, B is a moderate sure prize, and
their maximum pays for one setup cost. The decoy boxes only serve to separate A from B in the
reservation value order. They are chosen to have reservation values between those of A and B, but
their total expected reward is arbitrarily small.
Choose β with 1/2 < β < α. This will be the expected value of each useful box. Then choose
d > 0 such that β + d < α; d will upper-bound the total expected value of all decoys. Since β > 1/2,
choose p ∈(0, 1) small enough that
(2 −p)β > 1.
Finally choose ε > 0 small enough that
(2 −p)β −1 −2ε > 0
and
ε < β.
Next, we create the boxes. Box A has item cost cA = ε and
Pr[VA = β/p] = p,
Pr[VA = 0] = 1 −p.
Box B has item cost cB = ε and deterministic value VB = β. Thus
E[VA] = E[VB] = β.
Their reservation values are
σA = β −ε
p
,
σB = β −ε,
so σA > σB.
It remains to insert k boxes between A and B without giving a consecutive policy useful value.
Choose any target reservation value σD with σA > σD > σB. Each decoy is a rare high value: choose
G > max{σD, d/k}, let
Pr[VD = G] = d
kG,
Pr[VD = 0] = 1 −d
kG,
and set
cD = d
kG(G −σD).
Thus, each decoy box has expected value d/k. At the same time, its reservation value is exactly the
prescribed value σD, since
E[(VD −σD)+] = d
kG(G −σD) = cD.
We create independent copies D1, . . . , Dk of the same box type D.
Therefore the decreasing
reservation value order is
A ≻D1 ⪰· · · ⪰Dk ≻B.
Now consider any consecutive-batch policy π. The key point is that every nonempty batch pays
one setup cost, while a consecutive policy can extract at most one useful box, plus negligible decoy
box value, per opened batch. Let N be the number of nonempty batches opened, let IA, IB indicate
whether A, B are opened, and let IDj indicate whether the j-th decoy box is opened. If both A and
B are opened, then at least two batches must be opened: in the initial order, any interval containing
both useful boxes also contains all k decoys and therefore has size k + 2. Hence, pathwise,
IA + IB ≤N.
30


--- Page 31 ---
Also, if N = 0, no decoy box is opened, while if N ≥1, the total expected value of all opened decoy
boxes is at most the total expected value d of all decoys. Therefore, pathwise,
d

IDj ≤dN.

On the other hand, the unrestricted policy can open the non-consecutive batch {A, B}, which is
feasible because k ≥2. Since β/p > β,
E[max{VA, VB}] = p · β
p + (1 −p)β = (2 −p)β.
Therefore the original-cost value of opening {A, B} is
(2 −p)β −1 −2ε > 0.
Hence OPT1 > 0, while every consecutive-batch policy has α-discounted value at most zero. This
proves the theorem.
A.2
Numerical details for the strict adaptivity-gap example
We tuned parameters of the instance used in Example 3.1 with at most two decimal places. The setup
cost is T = 0.44, the batch capacity is k = 2, and the boxes are as follows. Box 1 is deterministic
and has value V1 = 0.83 and cost c1 = 0.40. Box 2 has distribution
Pr[V2 = 0] = 0.48,
Pr[V2 = 0.83] = 0.43,
Pr[V2 = 100] = 0.09,
and cost c2 = 8.50. Box 3 has distribution
Pr[V3 = 100] = 0.05,
Pr[V3 = 0] = 0.95,
and cost c3 = 4.16.
Consider the adaptive policy that first opens box 2. If V2 = 0, it opens {1, 3}. If V2 = 0.83, it
opens {3}. If V2 = 100, it stops. On the low and medium branches, the expected final reward after
opening the second batch is
0.05 · 100 + 0.95 · 0.83 = 5.7885.
31


--- Page 32 ---
Therefore the expected reward of the adaptive policy is
E[M] = (0.48 + 0.43) · 5.7885 + 0.09 · 100 = 14.267535.
The relevant batch costs are
K({2}) = 0.44 + 8.50 = 8.94,
K({1, 3}) = 0.44 + 0.40 + 4.16 = 5.00,
and
K({3}) = 0.44 + 4.16 = 4.60.
Hence
E[C] = 8.94 + 0.48 · 5.00 + 0.43 · 4.60 = 13.318.
Thus the adaptive policy has value
E[M] −E[C] = 0.949535.
We now compute the best fixed-menu value. Since a fixed-menu policy can ignore available
batches, it suffices to enumerate maximal disjoint menus. For each fixed menu F, we treat every
batch B ∈F as a Pandora box with reward XB = maxi∈B Vi and cost K(B), run Weitzman’s rule,
and record the resulting fixed-menu utility val1(F).
For k = 2, the maximal disjoint menus and their values are
F

Therefore
OPTfix(T, 2) = 0.796055.
Since
0.949535
0.796055 > 1.1928,
this gives a strict adaptivity gap of about 1.193.
For k ≥3, the only additional maximal menu is the single batch {{1, 2, 3}}. Its one-shot value is
E[max{V1, V2, V3}] −K({1, 2, 3}) = 14.267535 −13.50 = 0.767535,
which is still below 0.796055. Hence the same rounded instance gives a strict adaptive-versus-fixed-
menu gap for every k ≥2.
A.3
Capped-value reduction for non-reusable policies
For a feasible batch B, let XB = maxi∈B Vi. If K(B) = 0, define
κB = XB,
βB = 0.
If 0 < K(B) ≤E[XB], let σB solve
K(B) = E
(XB −σB)+.
For such positive-cost batches, define
κB = min{XB, σB},
βB = (XB −σB)+.
A positive-cost batch with K(B) > E[XB] is called overpriced.
32


--- Page 33 ---
Lemma A.2 (Overpriced Batches Can Be Skipped). In every finite non-reusable instance, there is
an optimal policy that never opens an overpriced batch.
Proof. Let W(U, m) be the optimal expected continuation payoff when the unopened boxes are U
and the current best observed value is m. Increasing the incumbent cannot hurt, and increasing it by
d can improve the final selected value by at most d. Thus W(U, ·) is nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz.
Suppose a policy is about to open an overpriced batch B ⊆U. Its continuation payoff is at most
−K(B) + EW(U \ B, max{m, XB}) ≤W(U \ B, m) −K(B) + E
(XB −m)+
≤W(U \ B, m) −K(B) + E[XB]
< W(U \ B, m).
Discarding B without opening it and then following the same continuation is therefore strictly
better than opening B.
Lemma A.3 (Capped-Value Upper Bound for Adaptive Policies). Let Oπ be the random family of
batches opened by a finite non-reusable policy π that uses no overpriced positive-cost batches. Then
val1(π) ≤E
max
␀{0} ∪{κB : B ∈Oπ}
 .
Proof. Index the possible rounds by t. Let Ht be the history immediately before round t, let It
indicate that the round is reached, and let Bt be the batch selected at that history. Both It and Bt
are Ht-measurable. Since Bt contains only unopened boxes, its primitive values are independent of
Ht. Therefore, on every reached history,
E[βBt | Ht] = E
(XBt −σBt)+ | Ht
 = K(Bt),
and hence E[It · βBt] = E[It · K(Bt)].

Proposition A.4 (Fixed Menus Are Classical Pandora Instances). Fix a finite disjoint family F
of feasible batches, each of which is either zero-cost or non-overpriced. Treat each batch B ∈F as
one box in a finite classical Pandora instance, with value distribution XB and opening cost K(B).
These induced boxes are independent, so Weitzman’s rule is optimal, and its value is

Proof. Disjointness makes the induced box prizes (XB)B∈F independent. The claim is Weitzman’s
theorem applied to these boxes [38].

A.4
Proof of the non-reusable adaptivity gap
Lemma A.5 (Random-Path Rounding). Let Y1, . . . , YN be independent latent variables. Each
action e has a support S(e) ⊆[N], reveals a measurable observation of (Yi)i∈S(e), and carries a
nonnegative integrable mark determined by that observation. Assume every feasible action sequence
has pairwise-disjoint supports. For every finite-depth adaptive decision tree, there is a deterministic
feasible path whose expected maximum mark is at least half the adaptive expected maximum mark.
Proof. It suffices to prove the claim for the randomized path obtained by running the tree on
an independent ghost instance and then probing the resulting path on a fresh real instance; one
deterministic path attains at least the average.
Fix a threshold τ ≥0. Let aτ(T ) be the probability that the adaptive tree T observes a mark at
least τ, and let rτ(T ) be the same probability for the ghost-path policy. We prove rτ(T ) ≥aτ(T )/2
by induction on the tree depth.
Let the root action be e, with mark Xe, observation Oe, and continuation tree To after observation
o. Put p = P[Xe ≥τ]. Then

gives

Proof of Theorem 3.2. The definitions above already handle zero-cost batches through κB = XB
and βB = 0. By Lemma A.2, take an optimal non-reusable policy that never opens an overpriced
positive-cost batch. Lemma A.3 upper-bounds its net value by the expected maximum capped value
among the batches it opens.
Apply Lemma A.5 to the adaptive decision tree whose actions are feasible batches, whose
supports are the primitive boxes in the batch, and whose mark is the capped value κB. Along
every realized non-reusable path these supports are disjoint. Hence some fixed disjoint family has
expected maximum capped value at least half the adaptive capped value. Proposition A.4 identifies
this quantity with the value of the corresponding fixed-menu Pandora instance. Thus

A.5
Proof of Theorem 3.3: Reusable reservation index
Proof of Theorem 3.3. For finite k, there are only
␀n+k
k
 −1 feasible reusable batches. For k = ∞,
every non-overpriced batch a satisfies
T +
X
i
ai · ci = K(a) ≤E[Xa] ≤Vmax.
Since every ci > 0, this implies ai ≤(Vmax −T)+/ci for each i, so only finitely many non-overpriced
batches remain. Hence σ⋆is attained whenever it is positive.
For every feasible reusable batch a and every s ≥σ⋆,
E
(Xa −s)+ ≤K(a).
For a non-overpriced batch this follows because the excess function decreases in s and s ≥σ(a). For
an overpriced batch it follows from E[(Xa −s)+] ≤E[Xa] < K(a).
Set W(m) = max{m, σ⋆}. If m < σ⋆, opening any batch a and then continuing according to W
gives at most
−K(a) + EW(max{m, Xa}) = σ⋆−K(a) + E
(Xa −σ⋆)+ ≤σ⋆= W(m).
If m ≥σ⋆, the corresponding bound is
−K(a) + E max{m, Xa} = m −K(a) + E
(Xa −m)+ ≤m = W(m).
Backward induction bounds every finite-horizon policy by W(m). For an admissible infinite-horizon
policy, truncate after h openings. Bounded convergence applies to the terminal reward and monotone
convergence applies to the accumulated cost, so the same upper bound survives as h →∞.
If σ⋆> 0, let a⋆attain it and put p = P[Xa⋆> σ⋆]. Positive opening cost implies p > 0.
Repeating a⋆until the first threshold crossing uses a geometric number of openings and has value
E[Xa⋆| Xa⋆> σ⋆] −K(a⋆)
p
= σ⋆,
by the reservation equation. This attains W(m) whenever m < σ⋆; for m ≥σ⋆, stopping attains
W(m).
